name: Rudolf and Snowflakes (hard version)
description: This is the hard version of the problem. The only difference is that in this version $$$n \le 10^{18}$$$. One winter morning, Rudolf was looking thoughtfully out the window, watching the falling snowflakes. He quickly noticed a certain symmetry in the configuration of the snowflakes. And like a true mathematician, Rudolf came up with a mathematical model of a snowflake. He defined a snowflake as an undirected graph constructed according to the following rules: Initially, the graph has only one vertex. Then, more vertices are added to the graph. The initial vertex is connected by edges to $$$k$$$ new vertices ($$$k \gt 1$$$). Each vertex that is connected to only one other vertex is connected by edges to $$$k$$$ more new vertices. This step should be done at least once . The smallest possible snowflake for $$$k = 4$$$ is shown in the figure. After some mathematical research, Rudolf realized that such snowflakes may not have any number of vertices. Help Rudolf check whether a snowflake with $$$n$$$ vertices can exist.
input_specification: The first line of the input contains an integer $$$t$$$ ($$$1 \le t \le 10^4$$$) — the number of test cases. Then follow the descriptions of the test cases. The first line of each test case contains an integer $$$n$$$ ($$$1 \le n \le 10^{18}$$$) — the number of vertices for which it is necessary to check the existence of a snowflake.
output_specification: Output $$$t$$$ lines, each of which is the answer to the corresponding test case — "YES" if there exists such $$$k \gt 1$$$ that a snowflake with the given number of vertices can be constructed; "NO" otherwise.

approach_summary: Verify predicate monotonicity: P(x) is true for x ≤ K and false otherwise. Binary search over the answer domain to find the boundary in O(log(Range) × Verify_Time).

topic_editorial.title: Editorial: 1846E2 — Rudolf and Snowflakes (hard version) [33. Binary Search]
topic_editorial.summary: Binary search on the monotonic answer domain.
topic_editorial.key_invariant: The predicate function $P(x)$ ('Is answer $\le x$ feasible?') is monotonic: if $P(x)$ is true for some value, it remains true for all larger values (or vice versa). This allows binary division of the answer search space $[\text{low}, \text{high}]$ in $O(\log(\text{Range}))$.
topic_editorial.complexity_analysis:
- **Time Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}(N \log(\text{Range}))$
  The binary search divides the search interval by 2 at each iteration, requiring $\log_2(\text{Range})$ steps. In each step, the feasibility check `check(mid)` scans the array in $\mathcal{O}(N)$ time.
- **Space Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}(1)$ auxiliary space
  The algorithm operates directly over the input array without allocating extra auxiliary memory.
